item.title: A Visual Guide to Precision-Recall Curves for Imbalanced Classification
item.dc:creator: James Mba Azam
item.description:
A common problem in machine learning classification is class imbalance: one class, often the one we care about (a disease case, a fraud, an outbreak), is far rarer than the other (Japkowicz and Stephen 2002; Guo et al. 2008; Ali et al. 2013; Abd Elrahman and Abraham 2013). In these cases the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve, which plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate across thresholds, can look excellent even when a model produces mostly false alarms. The precision-recall (PR) curve, which plots precision against recall, is more informative because it focuses on the rare class and gives no credit for correctly predicting the abundant one (Saito and Rehmsmeier 2015).

This article explores how the PR curve behaves under class imbalance, and gives guidance on reading it and avoiding common pitfalls. Every figure comes from a short script in scripts/ that uses synthetic data, so you can change the parameters and see what happens.

Quick start

pip install -r requirements.txt
python scripts/run_all.py        # regenerates every figure in figures/
python scripts/fig03_baseline.py # or run a single figure

About the data. All figures use a toy “binormal” model: negatives score ~ N(0, 1) and positives score ~ N(d, 1), where d sets how separable the classes are. It’s simple on purpose, so the only things changing between plots are the ones being discussed. Numbers quoted below come from these simulations, not from real datasets.

Measuring classifier performance

A binary classifier gives each case a score, and a decision threshold turns that score into a “positive” or “negative” prediction. Comparing the predictions with the truth sorts every case into one of four cells of a confusion matrix (Powers 2020):

Actually positive Actually negative
Predicted positive True positive (TP) False positive (FP)
Predicted negative False negative (FN) True negative (TN)

The common evaluation measures are ratios of these counts (Powers 2020):

  • Recall (also called sensitivity or true positive rate, TPR) = TP / (TP + FN): of the real positives, how many were caught.
  • Precision (also called positive predictive value) = TP / (TP + FP): of the cases flagged, how many were real.
  • False positive rate (FPR) = FP / (FP + TN): of the real negatives, how many were wrongly flagged. Specificity is 1 − FPR.
  • Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + FP + FN + TN): the share of all predictions that were correct.
  • F-beta score = (1 + β²) × precision × recall / (β² × precision + recall): a weighted harmonic mean of precision and recall, which is high only when both are. The parameter β sets how many times more important recall is than precision. Common choices are:
    • F1 (β = 1) = 2 × precision × recall / (precision + recall) weights the two equally.
    • F2 (β = 2) weights recall more heavily, which suits settings where missing a real positive is costlier than a false alarm, such as screening for a serious disease.
    • F0.5 (β = 0.5) weights precision more heavily, which suits settings where false alarms are costly, such as when each flagged case triggers an expensive follow-up.

Each of these is computed at one threshold. Sweeping the threshold from strict to lenient traces out a curve. The ROC curve plots TPR (recall) against FPR, and the PR curve plots precision against recall. Summary scores condense a curve into one number: ROC AUC is the area under the ROC curve, and average precision (AP) summarises the PR curve.

The denominators differ. Recall depends only on the real positives, FPR only on the real negatives, and precision on the cases flagged, which mix both classes. That difference matters when one class is rare.

1. Why not just use ROC?

With 1% positives, this model gets an ROC AUC of 0.96, which looks excellent. Its average precision is 0.47, and the PR curve shows precision falling steadily as recall rises.

The cause is the denominator. ROC uses the false positive rate, FP / (FP + TN). With 9,900 negatives in the denominator, many false alarms still give a small rate. Precision has no such cushion.

At this one threshold, the FPR is only 2%, but 225 false alarms are mixed in with 69 real hits, so only 23% of alerts are correct.

Script: fig01_roc_vs_pr.py, fig02_why_roc_hides_fp.py

2. The baseline is the prevalence, not 0.5

A random classifier draws a horizontal line at precision = positive rate. The three curves below come from classifiers of identical quality; only the class balance differs.

So a precision of 0.30 can be a strong result at 1% prevalence (30x chance) and a poor one at 50%. Always draw the baseline on your plot, and judge the curve by how far it sits above it.

Script: fig03_baseline.py

3. Reading the shape

Top-right is best. The shape tells you what trade-off you’re facing.

  • Steep decline: every extra bit of recall costs many false alarms. Typical for hard problems.
  • High plateau, then a cliff: a subset of positives is separated cleanly, so high-precision, low-recall use cases are feasible.
  • Jagged left edge: at very high thresholds only a few predictions are being judged, so a single mistake swings precision. Don’t over-read this region.

The curve is not guaranteed to be monotonic, unlike ROC.

Script: fig04_curve_shapes.py

4. Summarising with average precision (AP)

AP is the area under the PR curve, computed as a step-wise sum (sklearn.metrics.average_precision_score).

Linear interpolation between PR points (auc(recall, precision)) describes operating points you can’t actually reach, so it’s a biased estimate. The scikit-learn docs warn it can be too optimistic. In this small example it comes out lower (0.449 vs 0.516), so the safe summary is: prefer the step-wise version and don’t treat the two as interchangeable.

Also remember that AP is only meaningful relative to prevalence. An AP of 0.20 is excellent at 1% prevalence and mediocre at 30%, and APs aren’t comparable across datasets with different balance.

Script: fig05_ap_vs_trapezoid.py

5. Picking a threshold

  1. Decide what matters operationally: a minimum recall, or a minimum precision.
  2. Find that point on the curve and read off the threshold.
  3. Check the other axis. If it’s unacceptable, you need a better model or a relaxed constraint, not a different threshold.
  4. Choose the threshold on a validation set; report on a held-out test set.

Here, requiring 80% recall at 2% prevalence forces a threshold of about 1.58 and leaves precision at about 22%.

Script: fig06_threshold_picking.py

6. Worked example: what two operating points mean

Same model (2% prevalence), two thresholds, shown as alerts per 1,000 cases.

At 60% recall you review about 27 alerts and 12 are real. At 85% recall you catch 5 more real positives but review about 99 alerts. Whether that’s worth it depends on the cost of a miss versus the cost of reviewing a false alarm. The curve helps you make that call, which a single AUC cannot.

Script: fig11_worked_example.py

7. Pitfalls

Prevalence shift

Precision depends on class balance; recall doesn’t. If production prevalence differs from your evaluation set (for example, because you undersampled negatives), recompute or reweight precision using the true prior.

The same model and threshold has 79% recall everywhere, but precision is about 23% at 2% prevalence and about 3% at 0.2%.

Script: fig07_prevalence_shift.py

Resampling distorts probabilities

A common way to deal with class imbalance is to rebalance the training data. The Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) oversamples the rare class by creating synthetic cases, each placed at a random point on the line between a minority case and one of its nearest minority-class neighbours (Chawla et al. 2002). Undersampling does the opposite by discarding some of the abundant class. Either way, the training data no longer has the natural class distribution. This shifts the model’s predicted probabilities, so thresholds chosen on a resampled validation set won’t transfer.

After undersampling negatives, the model predicts 0.77 for a group of cases of which only about 20% are positive. Evaluate on data with the natural class distribution.

Script: fig08_resampling_calibration.py

Small positive counts

With few positives the curve is noisy. Use cross-validation or bootstrap bands, and report how many positives you have.

Script: fig09_small_sample_noise.py

Comparing models

A curve that dominates another everywhere is clearly better. When curves cross, the better model depends on which recall range you care about, and a single AP number hides that.

Script: fig10_model_comparison.py

  • Accuracy vs. Precision vs. Recall in Machine Learning: What is the Difference? by Encord. Link

Ali, Aida, Siti Mariyam Shamsuddin, and Anca L Ralescu. 2013. “Classification with Class Imbalance Problem.” Int. J. Advance Soft Compu. Appl 5 (3): 176–204.
Chawla, N. V., K. W. Bowyer, L. O. Hall, and W. P. Kegelmeyer. 2002. “SMOTE: Synthetic Minority Over-Sampling Technique.” Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 16 (June): 321–57. https://doi.org/10.1613/jair.953.

item.title: How to evaluate the ‘goodness of fit’ of an EpiNow2 model run
item.dc:creator: James Mba Azam
item.description:
library(EpiNow2)
library(posterior)
library(bayesplot)
library(data.table)
library(scoringutils)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

Introduction

This is a quick guide on how to assess or evaluate the output of an EpiNow2 model run.

TipEpiNow2 uses a Stan backend

{EpiNow2} uses Stan in the backend for model specification, fitting, and inference.

This means that the model fit can be assessed using the same tools and techniques used for any Stan model. The EpiNow2 package provides a convenient interface to run the models, but the underlying model is a Stan model.

The returned fit object is either a <stanfit> or CmdStanModel object, depending on the backend ({rstan} or {cmdstanr}) used. For example, you can use the {bayesplot} and {posterior} packages to visualize and summarize the model diagnostics.

Evaluating or assessing an {EpiNow2} model fit requires a holistic approach involving evaluating the MCMC diagnostics as well as the performance of the forecast against observed data. We will therefore proceed in that regard here.

Let’s start by setting up and running an example model, assessing the MCMC diagnostics, and then evaluating the forecast performance.

Running an example model

Input preparation

This will involve: loading required packages, setting up the model parameters, and running the model.

# Set number of cores for parallel processing.
options(mc.cores = min(4, parallel::detectCores() - 1))


# Set example generation time, incubation period, and reporting delay. In practice, these should use estimates from the literature or be estimated from data.
generation_time <- Gamma(
    shape = Normal(1.3, 0.3),
    rate = Normal(0.37, 0.09),
    max = 14
)

incubation_period <- LogNormal(
    meanlog = Normal(1.6, 0.06),
    sdlog = Normal(0.4, 0.07),
    max = 14
)
reporting_delay <- LogNormal(mean = 2, sd = 1, max = 10)

# Use example case data.

reported_cases <- example_confirmed[1:60]

# Plot the data
cases_plots <- ggplot(reported_cases, aes(x = date, y = confirm)) +
    geom_col() +
    labs(title = "Confirmed cases", x = "Date", y = "Cases") +
    theme_minimal()

cases_plots

Fitting the model

Estimate Rt and nowcast/forecast cases by date of infection.

out <- epinow(
    data = reported_cases,
    generation_time = gt_opts(generation_time),
    rt = rt_opts(prior = LogNormal(mean = 2, sd = 0.1)),
    delays = delay_opts(incubation_period + reporting_delay)
)
Logging threshold set at INFO for the name logger
Writing EpiNow2 logs to the console and:
'/var/folders/vr/dn4r1_zj417drd1zr9301trw0000gp/T//RtmpMm2rHx/regional-epinow/2020-04-21.log'.
Logging threshold set at INFO for the name logger
Writing EpiNow2.epinow logs to the console and:
'/var/folders/vr/dn4r1_zj417drd1zr9301trw0000gp/T//RtmpMm2rHx/epinow/2020-04-21.log'.
# Plot the model fit
plot(out)

Assessing model diagnostics

We’ll first extract the Stan fit object and compute diagnostics. The epinow() function returns a list of model outputs, including the Stan fit object. This is what we need to assess the model fit. Stan provides diagnostic metrics to assess the model fit, convergence, etc. which we’ll use to assess the model fit. The Stan ecosystem has a rich set of tools for diagnosing model fit, including the bayesplot and posterior packages. These tools provide a way to visualize and summarize the model diagnostics. For an indepth look at MCMC diagnostics, for example, see the bayesplot R package vignette on visual MCMC diagnostics. You can also do posterior predictive checks using the bayesplot package.

Diagnostics include:

  • Divergent transitions. These should be minimized; ideally 0. Divergent transitions can be improved by tuning Stan controls like adapt_delta, max_treedepth, and stepsize in stan_opts(). If there are divergent transitions, increase adapt_delta (e.g., 0.95 or 0.99). See an in‑depth explanation at https://mc-stan.org/learn-stan/diagnostics-warnings.html.
  • Rhat. These should be close to 1 indicating good mixing. Rhat values should be less than 1.05 (See ?rstan::Rhat).
  • Treedepth. This should be low; high values indicate potential issues with the model.
  • ESS values. These should be high; low values indicate insufficient sampling. In particular, both bulk‑ESS and tail‑ESS should be at least ~100 per chain to ensure reliable posterior quantile estimates (see ?rstan::ess_bulk).
fit <- out$estimates$fit

np <- bayesplot::nuts_params(fit)
divergence_data <- subset(np, Parameter == "divergent__")
treedepth_data <- subset(np, Parameter == "treedepth__")

posterior_summary <- posterior::summarize_draws(
    fit, c(posterior::default_convergence_measures(), "ess_basic")
) |> subset(variable != "lp__")

fit_ess_basic <- min(posterior_summary$ess_basic, na.rm = TRUE)
fit_ess_bulk <- min(posterior_summary$ess_bulk, na.rm = TRUE)
fit_ess_tail <- min(posterior_summary$ess_tail, na.rm = TRUE)

diagnostics <- data.table(
    "samples" = nrow(np) / length(unique(np$Parameter)),
    "max_rhat" = round(max(posterior_summary$rhat, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    "divergent_transitions" = sum(divergence_data$Value),
    "per_divergent_transitions" = mean(divergence_data$Value),
    "max_treedepth" = max(treedepth_data$Value),
    "ess_basic" = fit_ess_basic,
    "ess_bulk" = fit_ess_bulk,
    "ess_tail" = fit_ess_tail
)

diagnostics[, no_at_max_treedepth :=
                sum(treedepth_data$Value == max_treedepth)
][, per_at_max_treedepth := no_at_max_treedepth / samples]

knitr::kable(diagnostics)
samples max_rhat divergent_transitions per_divergent_transitions max_treedepth ess_basic ess_bulk ess_tail no_at_max_treedepth per_at_max_treedepth
2000 1.01 0 0 9 1325.989 1277.945 1109.327 837 0.4185

Evaluating forecast performance

Forecast performance can be evaluated by comparing the forecast of reported cases with the observed cases using Proper Scoring Rules(Gneiting and Raftery 2007; Carvalho 2016) such as the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) and Weighted Interval Score (WIS). These are available via the scoringutils::score() function.

The scoringutils::score() function requires a dataset that contains at least the following columns:

  • date: the date of the forecast
  • prediction: forecast values
  • true_value: the observed values
  • quantile: If evaluating quantiles, the quantile of the forecasted values (e.g., median, lower and upper bounds), in ascending order.

Let’s extract and prepare the forecasts and corresponding observed cases for the evaluation.

EpiNow2’s epinow() function returns a list of model outputs in the raw and several summarised formats for various use cases. In particular, there are time series of “infections”, “reported_cases”, “growth_rate”, and “R”, all grouped into “estimate”, “estimate based on partial data”, and “forecast”.

Here, we’re interested in the “forecast” type of the “reported_cases” variable, including the median and quantiles (lower and upper bounds).

# Extract the forecasts
forecasts <- out$estimates$summarised[variable == "reported_cases"][type == "forecast", ] %>% 
    select(-c(mean, sd, variable, strat, type))

Let’s also extract the corresponding subset of the observed data.

# Extract observed cases for the same period
obs_data <- example_confirmed[date >= min(forecasts$date) & date <= max(forecasts$date)]

Now, let’s combine the extracted forecasts with the observed data and clean up the quantiles into a format suitable for use with scoringutils. We will be cleaning them up because the forecasts data.table labels the quantiles as lower_20, upper_20, etc., where the number indicates the quantile level (e.g., 50% for the median), but that is not compatible with scoringutils.

# Combine forecasts with observed cases
eval_dt <- merge(forecasts, obs_data, by = "date")[, true_value := confirm][, confirm := NULL]

# Melt the data to long format
cols_to_melt <- c("median", grep("^(lower|upper)_", names(eval_dt), value = TRUE))
eval_long <- melt(
    eval_dt,
    id.vars = setdiff(names(eval_dt), cols_to_melt),
    measure.vars = cols_to_melt,
    variable.name = "prediction",
    value.name = "value"
)

# Prepare the evaluation data
eval_long[, quantile := fifelse(
  prediction == "median", 0.5,
  fifelse(
    grepl("^lower_", prediction),
    (1 - as.numeric(sub("lower_", "", prediction)) / 100) / 2,
    fifelse(
      grepl("^upper_", prediction),
      (1 + as.numeric(sub("upper_", "", prediction)) / 100) / 2,
      NA_real_
    )
  )
)][, prediction := value][, value := NULL]
Warning in fifelse(grepl("^lower_", prediction), (1 - as.numeric(sub("lower_",
: NAs introduced by coercion
Warning in fifelse(grepl("^upper_", prediction), (1 + as.numeric(sub("upper_",
: NAs introduced by coercion
# Sort the data by quantile
setorder(eval_long, quantile) %>% 
    head(10)
          date true_value prediction quantile
        <Date>      <num>      <num>    <num>
 1: 2020-04-22       2729    1526.00     0.05
 2: 2020-04-23       3370    1623.90     0.05
 3: 2020-04-24       2646    1911.95     0.05
 4: 2020-04-25       3021    1599.00     0.05
 5: 2020-04-26       2357    1701.95     0.05
 6: 2020-04-27       2324    1507.00     0.05
 7: 2020-04-28       1739    1237.85     0.05
 8: 2020-04-22       2729    1895.00     0.25
 9: 2020-04-23       3370    2056.75     0.25
10: 2020-04-24       2646    2420.00     0.25

Now we can use the scoringutils package to compute and summarise the scores. By default, a range of scores will be computed, including the interval_score, dispersion, underprediction, overprediction, coverage_deviation, bias, and ae_median.

# Mainly uses the scoringutils package
scored_scores <- eval_long[, quantile_level := quantile][, quantile := NULL][, model := "EpiNow2"] |> # align names to scoringutils preference
    as_forecast_quantile(observed  = "true_value", predicted = "prediction") |> 
    score() %>%
    summarise_scores()
Warning: ! Computation for `interval_coverage_90` failed. Error: ! To compute the
  interval coverage for an interval range of "90%", the 0.05 and 0.95 quantiles
  are required.
knitr::kable(scored_scores, digits = 3)
model wis overprediction underprediction dispersion bias interval_coverage_50 ae_median
EpiNow2 313.898 33.963 150.892 129.043 -0.143 0.571 444.286

Interpretation of scores

The table above provides a summary of the forecast performance by metrics. Note that it is not difficult to interpret the scores currently as they are not relative to other models. A proper comparison can only be done against other models.

TipComparing against a baseline model

A common practice is to have a baseline model (Stapper and Funk 2025), such as a naive model, and compare the scores of your model against it.

Future updates

In future updates, I will explore more advanced techniques for model diagnostics and evaluation, including posterior predictive checks, cross-validation, and more using packages like loo, shinystan, and bayesplot

Resources

As this is a simple and basic guide, I’ll direct you to the following resources for more in-depth information on model diagnostics and forecast evaluation.

  • Stan’s guide on How to Diagnose and Resolve Convergence Problems
  • Understanding, evaluating, and improving forecasts of infectious disease burden open course.
  • scoringutils R package documentation
  • scoringRules R package documentation
